question: Shared. Both studies ask whether naturalistic driving data, with demographics, can separate older drivers with MCI or dementia from cognitively healthy older drivers. P-331 uses 118 community drivers aged 65-90 in Nebraska (72 with MCI or dementia, 46 healthy aging). P-69 uses 2977 LongROAD drivers aged 65-79, of whom 61 were diagnosed with MCI, AD or another dementia during follow-up. The population class (older community drivers) and the comparison (cognitively impaired against healthy) match. The shared channel is naturalistic driving plus demographics: P-331's Model 4 uses exactly those inputs, and its headline Model 6 adds wrist actigraphy sleep. Allowed differences, recorded below as candidate explanations: timing (P-331 classifies status at baseline and also predicts status one year ahead; P-69's drivers were intact at enrolment and are labelled by the most severe diagnosis over up to 44 months of monitoring), label source, cohort, monitoring length and feature representation, architecture, sample size and validation design.
metric: Accuracy with accuracy (match); P-331 reports no AUC. Accuracy depends on the class mix, which is 61% impaired in P-331 and 14% impaired in P-69's test set. For that reason the prevalence-free balanced accuracy was also derived from each paper's printed figures.

figures.P-331: Subject-level accuracy from nested LOSO-CV with majority vote over weekly records. Model 6 (demographics + driving + sleep): 68.64% = 81/118, Wilson 95% CI [0.598, 0.763]. Model 4 (demographics + driving, the shared channel): 66.95% = 79/118, Wilson [0.581, 0.748]. One-year-ahead status (Model 6, n = 105 after 13 exclusions): 70.48% = 74/105, Wilson [0.612, 0.784]. Class-conditional rates derived from the printed precision and recall: Model 6 recall 75.00% = 54/72 and precision 73.97% give FP = 54/0.7397 - 54 = 19, so specificity = 27/46 = 0.587 (Wilson [0.443, 0.717]); balanced accuracy = (0.750 + 0.587)/2 = 0.668, SE = sqrt(0.25*(0.75*0.25/72 + 0.587*0.413/46)) = 0.044, CI [0.582, 0.755]. Model 4: recall 55/72, specificity 24/46 = 0.522, balanced accuracy 0.643, CI [0.556, 0.730].
figures.P-69: Interaction-based ResBlocks, Model 5 (demographics + driving time-series features + I-score), single random test set of 90 healthy and 15 impaired drivers. Accuracy 0.96 = 101/105 (confusion matrix 90 0 / 4 11), Wilson 95% CI [0.906, 0.985]; AUC 0.87 (no interval printed). Impaired-class recall = 11/15 = 0.733 (Wilson [0.481, 0.891]); healthy-class recall = 90/90 = 1.000 (Wilson [0.959, 1.000]). The paper labels these 'specificity 0.73' and 'sensitivity 1.0', so its sensitivity is computed on the healthy class. Balanced accuracy = (0.733 + 1.000)/2 = 0.867, SE = sqrt(0.25*(0.733*0.267/15 + 0.021^2)) = 0.058, CI [0.753, 0.980].

matched_figure_check: No printed figure reconciles the pair. On the shared channel, P-331's demographics-plus-driving Model 4 (66.95%, CI 0.581-0.748) is as far from P-69's 0.962 as the headline. On timing, P-331's one-year-ahead prediction, the design nearest P-69's forward-looking labels (70.48%, CI 0.612-0.784), is also far from it. Neither paper reports a result at the other's class mix. Derived from the printed counts, the prevalence-free comparison still differs. Balanced accuracy is 0.668 (CI 0.582-0.755) for P-331 and 0.867 (CI 0.753-0.980) for P-69. P-69's accuracy re-weighted to P-331's 61% prevalence is 0.61*0.733 + 0.39*1.000 = 0.837 (CI about 0.700-0.975), which lies outside P-331's [0.598, 0.763]. P-331's accuracy re-weighted to P-69's 14% prevalence is 0.143*0.750 + 0.857*0.587 = 0.610. The impaired-class detection rates agree (P-331 75.0%, P-69 73.3%); the gap lies in the healthy class, where P-69 misclassifies 0 of 90 healthy drivers and P-331 misclassifies 19 of 46.
performance_validity: Exclusion does not apply. P-69's accuracy of 0.962 is just below 0.97 and its AUC is 0.87, but the figure is internal, from one random split with only 15 impaired test cases, SMOTE-balanced training and no external cohort. P-331's 68.64% is internal nested LOSO-CV on 118 subjects. Neither estimate reaches 0.97 in the source.

candidate_explanations.difference: Class mix in the evaluation set: 14% impaired (15/105) in P-69 against 61% (72/118) in P-331. This accounts for part of the accuracy gap but not all of it: the balanced accuracies still differ (0.867 against 0.668).
candidate_explanations.quote: We randomly select 90 healthy and 15 dementia data points as the test data, and use the remaining 2826 healthy and 46 dementia data points as the training data.

candidate_explanations.difference: Timing and population behind the positive label: P-69's drivers were cognitively intact at enrolment and are labelled by the most severe diagnosis at any point in up to 44 months of monitoring; P-331 classifies clinician-assessed status at baseline.
candidate_explanations.quote: However, here we only use the most severe one. For instance, if one participant was healthy at the beginning of the study but gradually moved to MCI, unspecified dementia, and then Alzheimer’s disease, we will assign a value of one for this participant.

candidate_explanations.difference: Label source: P-331's status comes from comprehensive assessments by two dementia-specialist clinicians under the NIA-AA framework; P-69 uses yearly diagnosis labels from annual interviews.
candidate_explanations.quote: Note that throughout the study period, participants were interviewed annually. Thus, we have each participant’s yearly diagnosis label.

candidate_explanations.difference: Case mix of the impaired group: 25 of 61 have dementia in P-69 (8 AD, 17 other or unspecified), against 8 of 72 in P-331.
candidate_explanations.quote: Among these 61 patients, 36 have MCI, 8 Alzheimer’s disease, and 17 have other or unspecified dementia.

candidate_explanations.difference: Monitoring length and feature representation: 10 to 44 months of monthly driving variables, each summarised by 48 time-series features that capture change over time (P-69), against three months of weekly aggregated driving metrics (P-331).
candidate_explanations.quote: for each time-dependent driving variable, 48 time-series features are extracted using tsfeatures() package available in both R and Python [66].

candidate_explanations.difference: Monitoring length on P-331's side: three months at baseline.
candidate_explanations.quote: to continuously recorded naturalistic driving behavior over three months at baseline year.

candidate_explanations.difference: Validation and training design: P-69 uses one random split with 15 impaired test cases, SMOTE-balanced training and a module count chosen by AUC; P-331 uses nested leave-one-subject-out CV with subject-level majority voting.
candidate_explanations.quote: In this paper, we use SMOTE to balance the training data.
The Outer CV Loop used Leave-One-Subject-Out Cross-Validation (LOSOCV) to evaluate generalization performance

candidate_explanations.difference: Sample size and classifier: about 2872 training drivers (46 impaired) with an ensemble of interaction-based residual blocks on I-score-selected modules (P-69), against about 117 training drivers per fold with XGBoost (P-331).
candidate_explanations.quote: The model with the highest AUC is identified, and the corresponding number of modules is recorded.

reason: Both papers ask whether naturalistic driving data can identify older drivers with MCI or dementia. Their accuracies differ well beyond uncertainty: 0.962 (CI 0.906-0.985) against 0.686 (CI 0.598-0.763), and 0.670 on P-331's matched driving-plus-demographics inputs. The gap survives the prevalence difference: the balanced accuracies are 0.867 against 0.668, and the difference lies in how many healthy drivers each model misclassifies. The pair qualifies as an unresolved discrepancy. The listed differences (class mix, label timing and source, case mix, monitoring length, validation design) may explain it, but neither paper shows that any one of them is sufficient.

quotes.quote: Due to the small number of participants classified as dementia (N = 8), this group combined with those classified as MCI (N = 64) to form a single unified cognitive impairment group (N = 72). The remaining participants (N = 46) were classified as the healthy aging.
Finally, the model 6 integrating demographics, driving performance, driving life-space, and sleep data achieved the highest accuracy (68.64%), precision (73.97%), and F1-score (74.48%).
Accuracy increased from 68.64% to 70.48%, and recall from 75.00% to 77.97%, while precision slightly decreased from 73.97% to 71.88%
Interestingly, a model using only demographics and driving features achieved the highest recall (76.39%), suggesting their strong association with cognitive status.
Participants with cognitive decline but without substantial functional impairments were classified as having MCI.
We computed multiple metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, at the driver level rather than at the weekly observation level.
Naturalistic driving trajectories were collected through in-vehicle recording devices for up to 44 months from 2977 participants who were cognitively intact at the time of enrollment.
our proposed classification method achieves the best accuracy (96%) for predicting MCI and dementia
Accuracy may no longer be a good metric to evaluate the performance of a classifier over an imbalanced dataset, because it is biased toward the majority class.
a confusion matrix is also evaluated over 90 healthy and 15 dementia test data
